\section[vigente]{vigente — in force, current}

\label{lesson:ES-C625-vigente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the certificate, then the Spanish for official.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vigente}
\textbf{vigente} — \textquotedblleft{}in force, current\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Esta ley ya no está vigente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This law is no longer in force.}
\end{quote}

For laws, rules and prices.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vigente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{vigens} 'thriving, strong' (EtymDB), from \emph{vigere} 'to be lively'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vigente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vigente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{vigente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the certificate, then the Spanish for official, then say \emph{vigente} again
\end{itemize}

What does vigente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}In force, current\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[ilegal]{ilegal — illegal}

\label{lesson:ES-C625-ilegal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for official, then the Spanish for in force.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ilegal}
\textbf{ilegal} — \textquotedblleft{}illegal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aparcar aquí es ilegal.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Parking here is illegal.}
\end{quote}

The opposite of \emph{legal}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ilegal} is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin \emph{illegalis}, built from \emph{in-} 'not' and \emph{legalis}, from \emph{lex} 'law' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ilegal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ilegal}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ilegal}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for official, then the Spanish for in force, then say \emph{ilegal} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does ilegal mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Illegal\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[infringir]{infringir — to break, to infringe}

\label{lesson:ES-C625-infringir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for in force, then the Spanish for illegal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: infringir}
\textbf{infringir} — \textquotedblleft{}to break, to infringe\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Infringió las normas del club.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He broke the club rules.}
\end{quote}

Formal, for rules and laws. Spelling: \emph{infrinjo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{infringir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{infringere} 'to break, to weaken', built from \emph{in} and \emph{frangere} 'to break' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{infringir}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{infringir}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for in force, then the Spanish for illegal, then say \emph{infringir} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[denunciar]{denunciar — to report; to denounce}

\label{lesson:ES-C625-denunciar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for illegal, then the Spanish for to break.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: denunciar}
\textbf{denunciar} — \textquotedblleft{}to report; to denounce\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Denuncié el robo a la policía.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I reported the theft to the police.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Denunciar} to the police is to make a formal report.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{denunciar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{denuntiare} 'to announce, to give notice', built on \emph{nuntius} 'messenger' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{denunciar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{denunciar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{denunciar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for illegal, then the Spanish for to break, then say \emph{denunciar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does denunciar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To report; to denounce\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la denuncia]{la denuncia — the report, the complaint}

\label{lesson:ES-C625-denuncia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to break, then the Spanish for to report.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la denuncia}
\textbf{la denuncia} — \textquotedblleft{}the report, the complaint\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Puse una denuncia en la policía.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I made a report to the police.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Poner una denuncia} — to file a report.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{denuncia} is built on \emph{denunciar}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{denuntiare} 'to announce', from \emph{nuntius} 'messenger' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la denuncia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to break, then the Spanish for to report, then say \emph{la denuncia} again
\end{itemize}
